---
title: Writing Style
---

These are the rules this documentation follows. They were derived from the
[Refactor Arena](https://refactorarena.com/) documentation so that the two
projects read the same way, and they apply to every page under `docs/`.


## Voice

- Write in the present tense, about the system: "The verifier applies the rule
  named in the header." Describe what the software does, not what it will do.
- Address the reader as "you" only in instructions and tutorials. Never write
  "we".
- State facts plainly. Do not hedge with "simply", "just", or "easily", and do
  not sell.
- Prefer one idea per sentence. Sentences average about twenty words; a long
  sentence is fine when it carries one idea, and a short one is fine when it
  carries a warning.
- Contractions are acceptable in prose ("it's", "don't"), not in reference
  material.
- Use "for instance" and "e.g." for examples, in parentheses when the example
  is short: "(e.g., `alice@example.com`)".
- No Oxford comma: "unit, integration and end-to-end tests".


## Page Structure

- Every page starts with YAML front matter carrying `title`. The body has no
  level-one heading; the title is it.
- The first paragraph is a lead: one or two sentences saying what the page
  covers and why it matters. Then the sections.
- Sections are level-two headings in Title Case ("Getting Started", "Run a
  Basic Eval"). Subsections are level three; option groups and small
  divisions are level four. Do not go deeper.
- Leave two blank lines before every level-two heading and one before lower
  headings.
- Hard-wrap prose at 100 columns. Code blocks and tables are exempt.
- End index-style pages with a "Learning More" section: a bulleted list of
  links, each followed by a colon and a one-line description of the page.


## Lists

- Use a definition list (a term on one line, the definition on the next
  starting with `: `) for terminology, CLI options, and any set of named
  things with a sentence of explanation each. Indent continuation lines by two
  spaces.
- Use a bulleted list for parallel items. When each item names something,
  bold the name and follow it with a colon: `- **Term**: description`. When
  each item is a link, use the link as the name: `- [Page](page.qmd): what it
  covers`.
- Use a numbered list for steps. Put a code block under a step when the step
  is a command.
- Keep each item to a sentence or two. A paragraph belongs outside the list.


## Code and Names

- Put file names, commands, flags, field names and values in backticks.
- Give every code block a language. Bash blocks may open with a `#` comment
  saying what the command does.
- Show real output where the page is about output. Do not invent values;
  copy them from a run.
- Name the header fields by their short JOSE names (`alg`, `kid`, `iss`) and
  expand each the first time a page uses it.


## Cross-References

- Link to other pages by relative `.qmd` path: `[Verifier](../components/verifier.qmd)`.
  Link to a section with a fragment: `[Statuses](verifier.qmd#statuses)`.
- Link external standards inline the first time they are named, with the RFC
  number in the text: "[RFC 7797](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7797)".
- Class and function names in backticks link to the reference automatically
  when the reference page documents them; do not hand-link them.


## Callouts

Use Quarto callouts sparingly, one per section at most:

- `.callout-note` for a fact the reader might otherwise miss.
- `.callout-tip` for a shortcut or a recommended practice.
- `.callout-important` for something that changes what the reader must do,
  such as the dev-mode warning.
- `.callout-warning` for a security consequence.


## Terminology

Define a term once, on the [Definitions](../guide/basics/concepts.qmd) page,
and use it consistently after that. In particular:

- "signed instruction block", or "block" once the context is clear; never
  "SIB block" or "envelope" outside the format specification.
- "signer" for the human, "harness" for the runtime that executes tool calls,
  "classifier" for the model that decides whether an action may run, and
  "verifier" for the deterministic component that checks signatures.
- "verified" only for a block whose status is `verified`. A block that failed
  is described by its status, never as "invalid" alone.
- "dev mode" and "enforced mode", not "test mode" or "production mode".


## Specification Pages

The specification uses the same voice with two additions. Requirements use
the [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119) keywords MUST, MUST
NOT, SHOULD and MAY in capitals, and each normative rule stands in its own
sentence so it can be cited. Algorithms are numbered lists whose steps each
name the status they produce on failure.
